skal.summary: Modal verb (present of skulle). Never "go", and rarely English "shall" — it depends on context:

uses.da: Jeg skal til Aarhus i morgen.

uses.en: a promise: I'll make sure to
don't need to — or a friendly "don't" (context decides)
uses.da_en: You don't need to pay anything.

skal.note: With a destination the motion verb is left out: "Jeg skal hjem" = I'm going home. "Skal vi ikke …?" = Shall we / Why don't we …? (ikke is not a negation; answer jo). Hearsay: "Han skal være rig" = He's supposed to be rich. For an unmistakable "don't have to" use behøver ikke. (Also a noun: en skal = a shell, peel, skin.)

skulle.summary: Modal verb: skal (present) · skulle (past) · har skullet. Very often "should" — not just the past of skal:

uses.da: Vi skulle til Aarhus, men toget blev aflyst.
uses.da_en: We were going to Aarhus, but the train was cancelled.

uses.da: Du skulle prøve den nye café.
uses.da_en: You should try the new café.

uses.en: should have / was supposed to (but didn't)
uses.da: Jeg skulle have ringet i går.

uses.da_en: The film is supposed to be good.

uses.da: Hvis du skulle få brug for hjælp, så ring.
uses.da_en: If you should need any help, call.

skulle.note: For the present-tense uses (plans, duties, offers, ordering) see skal. Advice with skulle is softer than bør.

vil.summary: Modal verb (present of ville). Mostly WANT. English "will" is usually just the present tense; vil = "will" only in predictions (more formal).

uses.da: Jeg vil gerne have en kaffe.

uses.en: do you want to…? / would you like to…?
uses.da_en: Do you want to come to the cinema?

uses.da: Det vil tage et par uger.
uses.da_en: It will take a couple of weeks.

vil.note: Your own plans and promises are not vil: "Jeg ringer i morgen" = I'll call tomorrow; "Det regner i morgen" = It will rain tomorrow; plans take skal. "Jeg vil komme" sounds like "I want to / insist on coming". vil have + noun = want (blunt): "Vil du have kaffe?" With a place no verb is needed: "Jeg vil gerne til Mexico."

ville.summary: Modal verb: vil (present) · ville (past) · har villet. The past of "want" — and English "would":

uses.da: Jeg ville bare høre, om du vil med.
uses.da_en: I just wanted to ask if you'd like to come.

uses.da: Jeg ville have hjulpet dig, hvis du havde spurgt.
uses.da_en: I would have helped you if you'd asked.

uses.da: Jeg ville ønske, at jeg kunne rejse.

ville.note: For the present-tense uses see vil.

kan.summary: Modal verb (present of kunne): can, be able to — plus a few uses English says differently:

uses.da: Jeg kan desværre ikke i morgen.
uses.da_en: Unfortunately I can't make it tomorrow.

uses.en: certainly can (godt confirms; it does NOT mean "well")
can you…? / could you…? (ikke is not a negation)

kan.note: Past: kunne (could). "Det kan godt være" = Maybe / That may well be. "Kunne godt tænke sig" = would like: "Jeg kunne godt tænke mig en kop te."

kunne.summary: Modal verb: kan (present) · kunne (past) · har kunnet.

uses.da: Vi kunne tage ud og spise.
uses.da_en: We could go out to eat.

uses.da: Jeg kunne godt tænke mig at rejse.

kunne.note: "Kunne du tænke dig …?" = Would you like …? For the present-tense uses see kan.

må.summary: Modal verb (present of måtte): permission — and sometimes necessity.

uses.en: yes, go ahead / you're welcome to

uses.da: Du må hellere ringe til lægen.
Det må være dejligt at bo ved havet.
uses.da_en: It must be lovely to live by the sea.

må.note: "Må jeg få…?" is the polite way to ask for something. Watch out: "må ikke" is a prohibition, not "don't have to" (that is "behøver ikke"). må = your own need; skal = a rule or plan. "Du må undskylde" = I'm sorry / please forgive me.

måtte.summary: Modal verb: må (present) · måtte (past) · har måttet.

uses.da_en: I had to take a taxi.

måtte.note: For the present-tense uses see må. (Also a noun: en måtte = a mat.)

bør.summary: Modal verb (present of burde): should, ought to — a recommendation.
bør.note: No "at" after it. Past and softer form: burde. "Det burde du have gjort" = You should have done that. Advice with skal can sound like an order; bør, burde and skulle are advice.

gider.summary: Present of gide. No neat English verb: "can be bothered to", "feel like".

uses.en: can't be bothered to, don't feel like
uses.da: Jeg gider ikke gå ud i aften.
uses.da_en: I can't be bothered to go out tonight.

uses.da: Gider du lige række mig saltet?
uses.da_en: Would you mind passing me the salt?

uses.da: Jeg gider ikke høre mere om det.
uses.da_en: I don't want to hear any more about it.

gider.note: Forms: gide · gider · gad · har gidet. Like a modal verb, no "at". gider ikke = no desire; vil ikke sounds like a firm refusal; orker ikke = no energy. Casual: skip it in formal writing, and with a sharp tone a request can sound irritated.

tør.summary: Two different words: the adjective "dry", and the present of turde (dare).
tør.note: Verb: turde · tør · turde · har turdet. Adjective: tør · tørt · tørre. Not tørre (to dry), whose past is tørrede.

bliver.summary: Present of blive. One of the most useful Danish verbs — no single English match:

uses.da: Jeg bliver altid sulten om eftermiddagen.
uses.da_en: I always get hungry in the afternoon.

uses.en: will be, is going to be

uses.da_en: The parcel is being sent today.

uses.da: Hun bliver ved med at ringe.

bliver.note: Forms: blive · bliver · blev · er blevet (perfect takes "er"). er = a state, blive = a change: "Jeg er glad" (I'm happy) / "Jeg blev glad, da han ringede" (It made me happy when he called). Ages: "Hun bliver 30 næste år" = She'll turn 30 next year. For the price of one item use koster; for the total, bliver.

blive.summary: Verb: blive · bliver · blev · er blevet. Become, get, stay — see bliver for all the uses.

uses.da_en: He wants to become a doctor.
Can you stay a bit longer?

blive.note: Perfect with "er": "Hun er blevet mor" (She has become a mother). "Get + adjective" is blive, not få: blive træt, blive gift.

får.summary: Present of få (get) — and a few uses English says differently:

uses.da: Må jeg få et glas vand?
uses.da_en: Could I have a glass of water?

uses.da: Han får lov til at gå.
Jeg får det gjort i morgen.
Hun får mig altid til at grine.

får.note: Forms: få · får · fik · har fået. "Get + adjective" is blive (blive træt = get tired), not få. "Må jeg få…?" goes with få; vil goes with have: "Vil du have kaffe?" Also a noun: et får = a sheep.

gerne.summary: No English equivalent — it marks that something is wanted or welcome.

uses.da: Du må gerne låne min cykel.
uses.da_en: Feel free to borrow my bike.

uses.da: Ring gerne, hvis du har spørgsmål.
uses.da_en: Feel free to call if you have any questions.

uses.da: Om søndagen sover vi gerne længe.
uses.da_en: On Sundays we usually sleep in.

gerne.note: Danish has no word for "please"; gerne, lige and tak do that job. gerne goes with vil (and må); with kan use godt: "Jeg kan godt". Comparison: gerne · hellere (rather) · helst (most of all, preferably).

uses.da_en: I can speak French (I really can).

uses.da: Jeg ved godt, det er dyrt.

godt.note: "Kan godt lide" = like. "Det kan godt være" = maybe, that may be. "Godt nok" = admittedly / really (see nok). "Hav det godt!" = Take care!

henne.summary: A place word with no English translation — leave it out when translating.
henne.note: Pair with hen (movement): "Hvor skal du hen?" = Where are you going? Like hjem (to home) vs hjemme (at home). derhenne = over there.

hos.summary: Preposition: at someone's place — like French "chez".

uses.da: Vi spiser hos mine forældre på søndag.
uses.da_en: We're eating at my parents' on Sunday.

uses.da: Han bor stadig hos sin mor.
uses.da_en: He still lives with his mother.

hos.note: Being there = hos; going there = til: "Jeg går til lægen" (I'm going to the doctor). "Hjemme hos mig" = at my place.

synes.summary: "Think" as in an OPINION from your own experience. Danish splits English "think" several ways:

uses.da_en: I think the film is good.

uses.da: Jeg tror, han kommer i morgen.

synes.note: Test: can it be checked or known later? tror. Is it your taste or judgement? synes. "Jeg tror, det er en god film" = I haven't seen it; "Jeg synes, det er en god film" = I've seen it. "Jeg tænker, at …" for an opinion is common now but some dislike it; synes is the safe choice. Forms: synes · synes · syntes · har syntes (no -r in the present).

tror.summary: Present of tro: "think" as in BELIEVE or GUESS — something that could turn out true or false.

uses.en: I think so / I don't think so

tror.note: For an opinion or taste use synes: "Jeg synes, det er dyrt" (I think it's expensive). Forms: tro · tror · troede · har troet.

mener.summary: Present of mene: mean — or hold an opinion (stronger than synes).

uses.en: think, believe, be of the view
uses.da: Hun mener, at skatten er for høj.
uses.da_en: She thinks taxes are too high.

uses.da: Hun kommer på mandag – jeg mener tirsdag.
uses.da_en: She's coming on Monday – I mean Tuesday.

har.summary: Present of have: have — and the helper verb for the past (perfect).

uses.da: Jeg har boet her i tre år.
uses.da_en: I've lived here for three years.

har.note: Verbs of movement or change usually take er when the result matters: er kommet, er blevet, "Han er gået" (he's left) — but "Han har gået meget i dag" (he's walked a lot today). "Hvordan har du det?" = How are you? "Hvornår har du fødselsdag?" = When's your birthday?

sin.summary: "His/her own" — points back to the subject. English has no matching word.
sin.note: sin (en-word) · sit (et-word) · sine (plural). Only for a 3rd-person singular subject (also man); with "de" use deres. Inside the subject itself use hans/hendes: "Han og hans bror kom."

plejer.summary: Present of pleje: "usually" — Danish uses a verb where English uses an adverb.

uses.da: Jeg plejer at cykle på arbejde.
Vi plejede at tage til Skagen hver sommer.
uses.da_en: We used to go to Skagen every summer.

uses.da: Vi ses klokken otte, som vi plejer.
uses.da_en: See you at eight, as usual.

plejer.note: Also: pleje = to care for / nurse someone, and en plejer = a carer.

hygge.summary: A Danish concept: relaxed, warm, unpretentious time — usually together. Learn it as Danish.

uses.en: a nice relaxed time, cosiness, good atmosphere
uses.da: Der var rigtig god hygge til festen.
uses.da_en: The party had a really nice, relaxed atmosphere.

uses.da: Vi hygger os med en film.

uses.da_en: Have a great time in Berlin!

uses.da: Det var hyggeligt at se dig!
uses.da_en: It was lovely to see you!

hygge.note: Not just candles and blankets: a busy café or a barbecue can be hyggeligt. Often it simply means "having a nice time", so translate by context.

hyggelig.summary: Adjective from hygge: nice, cosy, pleasant — used about places, people and time together.

uses.da: Det var hyggeligt at se dig.
uses.da_en: It was nice to see you.

hyggelig.note: "Det var hyggeligt!" is the standard thank-you after meeting up. About people English says nice or pleasant, never "cosy". Opposite: uhyggelig = creepy, scary.

pyt.summary: A small Danish attitude word: let it go.

uses.da: Vi missede bussen, men pyt, vi tager den næste.
uses.da_en: We missed the bus, but oh well, we'll get the next one.

pyt.note: For small setbacks only — said about someone else's real problem it sounds like "who cares". (Also: en vandpyt = a puddle.)

orke.summary: To have the energy for something — mostly in the negative.

uses.en: can't face, don't have the energy
uses.da: Jeg orker ikke at lave mad i aften.

uses.da_en: Are you up for a walk?

orke.note: Close to gider, but about energy rather than motivation, and stronger: gider ikke = no desire, orker ikke = no energy left. Forms: orke · orker · orkede · har orket.

træls.summary: Annoying, tedious — originally Jutlandic, now used all over Denmark (casual).

uses.da: Det er træls, at bussen er forsinket.
uses.da_en: It's annoying that the bus is late.
Washing up is a tedious chore.

træls.note: Used about situations and tasks, not people. Too casual for formal writing.

tak.summary: Thanks — Danes say tak in many set phrases English doesn't have:

uses.en: don't mention it / thank YOU (when it was mutual)
uses.da: Det var så lidt. / Selv tak!

tak.note: "Ja tak" = yes please; "nej tak" = no thanks. The reply to "tak for mad" is velbekomme. Danish has no single word for "please": tak, gerne, lige and "vil du være sød at …" do the job.

lige.summary: One of the most common Danish words; the meaning depends on stress and position:

uses.da_en: Could you give me a quick hand?

uses.da: Kaffe eller te? – Det er lige meget.
uses.da_en: Coffee or tea? – I don't mind.

uses.da: Han er lige så høj som sin far.
uses.da_en: He's as tall as his father.

lige.note: "Lige nu" = right now; "lige om lidt" = in a moment; "lige før" = just before; "Vent lige!" = hang on! "I lige måde" = likewise, same to you. Leaving lige out of a request can sound abrupt.

uses.da: Der er en bus klokken tre.

der.note: "It" is den or det: "Hvor er bilen? Den er her." "Der står …" = It says … (in writing).

nogen.summary: "Any" or "some(one)" — choosing between nogen, noget and nogle:
nogen.note: nogen and nogle sound the same ("NO-en"). A handy test: if you could add "at all" (som helst), write nogen. In questions nogle is also possible and means "a few": "Skal du ikke have nogle nye sko?"

gift.summary: Two words: married (adjective, the common one) — and poison (noun). Not English "gift" — a present is en gave.

uses.da: Hun er gift med en svensker.

jo.summary: Two jobs: the "yes" to a negative question, and a little word meaning "as you know / after all":

uses.da: Kan du ikke lide kaffe? – Jo!
uses.da_en: Don't you like coffee? – Yes, I do!

uses.da: Han er jo kun fire år.
Jeg kan ikke komme, jeg skal jo arbejde.
uses.da_en: I can't come — I have to work, you know.

jo.note: After a negative question "ja" sounds wrong — say jo. The "you know" jo is unstressed and never first in the sentence; used about something the listener didn't know, it can sound condescending.

vel.summary: "I suppose / …, right?" — a guess that asks for agreement:

uses.da: Du kunne vel ikke låne mig hundrede kroner?
uses.da_en: You couldn't lend me a hundred kroner, could you?

vel.note: Unstressed. "…, ikke?" sounds more confident; vel more tentative. Stressed vel = well (formal): vel forberedt = well prepared.

nok.summary: Unstressed: "probably, I think". Stressed: "enough". And skal nok = "I promise / it'll be fine":

uses.en: it'll be fine / I will, I promise
uses.da: Bare rolig, det skal nok gå.

nok.note: "Jeg kommer nok" = I'll probably come — a hedge, not a promise. "Det tror jeg nok" = I think so (or, ironic, I'll bet!). nok = your own guess; vist = something you've heard.

da.summary: Three different words: "when" (one past event), "since / as", and a little word adding "surely / come on":

uses.da: Da jeg var barn, boede vi i Aalborg.
uses.da_en: When I was a child, we lived in Aalborg.

uses.da: Da det regner, bliver vi hjemme.
uses.da_en: As it's raining, we're staying home.

uses.da: Hold da op, hvor er her flot!

da.note: For repeated or future "when" use når; for questions hvornår. The insisting da is unstressed and never first in the sentence.

dog.summary: "However, though" in writing — and emotional emphasis in speech:

uses.da: Vejret var dog fint om eftermiddagen.
uses.da_en: The weather was fine in the afternoon, though.
Well I never, is that you?

dog.note: Not the English word — a dog is en hund.

mon.summary: "I wonder" — turns a question into thinking out loud. No one-word English equivalent.

uses.da_en: I wonder if he's coming tonight.

uses.en: I should think so! / You bet!
uses.da_en: Is she coming? – I should think so!

uses.da: Mon ikke vi skal gå nu?
uses.da_en: Don't you think we should go now?

mon.note: "Mon ikke" signals near-certainty, not doubt. No subject before it: "Mon det regner i morgen?", never "Jeg mon …".

sgu.summary: Adds punch: "honestly, really, damn". Mild swearing (from "så Gud", so help me God):
sgu.note: Fine among friends; skip it in formal speech and writing. It goes before ikke: "sgu ikke".

vist.summary: "Apparently, I think" — you've heard it or noticed it, but you're not sure:

uses.da: Han er vist syg i dag.

uses.da_en: I think that's her over there.

uses.da: Må jeg låne den? – Ja vist!
uses.da_en: Can I borrow it? – Of course!

vist.note: nok = your own estimate; vist = something you've heard or seen. Not to be confused with vise (to show).

altså.summary: Not English "also" (that's også). So, that is, I mean — and spoken emphasis:

uses.da: Vi ses på fredag, altså den 12.
uses.da_en: See you on Friday — I mean, the 12th.

uses.da: Det er altså ikke i orden.
Altså, jeg ved det ikke helt.

altså.note: In writing it also means "therefore". Danes use it constantly in speech.

behøve.summary: Need (to) — mostly in the negative: behøver ikke = don't have to.

uses.en: don't have to, no need to
uses.da: Du behøver ikke (at) tage skoene af.
uses.da_en: You don't need to take your shoes off.

uses.da: Skal jeg hjælpe dig? – Nej, det behøver du ikke.
uses.da_en: Shall I help you? – No, there's no need.

uses.da: Behøver jeg at komme i morgen?
uses.da_en: Do I need to come tomorrow?

behøve.note: Forms: behøve · behøver · behøvede · har behøvet; "at" is optional. Don't confuse with "må ikke", which forbids. For a positive "have to" Danes say "er nødt til (at)" or skal: "Jeg er nødt til at gå."

komme.summary: Come — plus komme til at, which has little to do with "come":

uses.da: Det kommer til at tage lang tid.
uses.da_en: It's going to take a long time.

uses.da: Undskyld, jeg kom til at tage din kop.
uses.da_en: Sorry, I took your cup by mistake.

uses.da: Jeg kom aldrig til at se Paris.
uses.da_en: I never got to see Paris.

uses.da: Jeg kommer for sent i dag.
uses.da_en: I'm going to be late today.

uses.da: Tak for i aften! – Kom godt hjem!
uses.da_en: Thanks for tonight! – Get home safely!

komme.note: Forms: komme · kommer · kom · er kommet (perfect with er). Often just future: "Jeg kommer i morgen" = I'll come tomorrow. "Jeg kom til at …" almost always means you did it by mistake.

være.summary: Be — but Danish separates a state (være) from a change (blive), and uses "være ved at" for "-ing":

uses.da: Jeg blev overrasket, da han ringede.
uses.da_en: I was surprised when he called.

uses.when: være ved at / i gang med
uses.da: Han er i gang med at skrive.

uses.da_en: Do you want to join in?

uses.en: be — Danes often say ligger / står

være.note: Forms: være · er · var · har været. er also forms the perfect of verbs of movement and change: "Han er gået" (he's left), "Hun er blevet læge". Never er before another verb: "Jeg taler dansk", not "Jeg er taler".

ved.summary: Two different words: the preposition "by / at", and the present of vide (know):

uses.da: Jeg ved godt, at jeg er sent på den.
Vi har et sommerhus ved vandet.
uses.da_en: We have a summer house by the water.

uses.da: Jeg er ved at lave mad.

ved.note: The "know" ved needs an object: "Det ved jeg" / "Jeg ved det", never just "Jeg ved". People and places take kende: "Kender du Mette?" "Det gode ved det er …" = The good thing about it is …

vide.summary: Know a FACT. Danish has three "know"s: vide (facts), kende (people, places), kunne (skills, languages).

uses.da_en: Do you know where she lives?

uses.da: Hvornår får vi det at vide?

vide.note: Forms: vide · ved · vidste · har vidst. Never "Jeg ved" on its own, and never "vider". "Jeg ved ham" → "Jeg kender ham".

kende.summary: Know a PERSON, PLACE or THING (be familiar with). For facts use vide (ved).

uses.da: Jeg vil gerne lære dig bedre at kende.
uses.da_en: I'd like to get to know you better.

uses.da: Jeg kan ikke kende forskel på dem.
Det er svært at stå op om vinteren. – Det kender jeg godt!
uses.da_en: It's hard to get up in winter. – I know the feeling!

kende.note: Forms: kende · kender · kendte · har kendt. Facts take vide: "Jeg kender hende, men jeg ved ikke, hvor hun bor." (Also a noun: en kender = an expert, connoisseur.)

kender.summary: Know a PERSON, PLACE or THING (be familiar with). For facts use vide (ved).

uses.da: Jeg vil gerne lære dig bedre at kende.
uses.da_en: I'd like to get to know you better.

uses.da: Jeg kan ikke kende forskel på dem.
Det er svært at stå op om vinteren. – Det kender jeg godt!
uses.da_en: It's hard to get up in winter. – I know the feeling!

kender.note: Forms: kende · kender · kendte · har kendt. Facts take vide: "Jeg kender hende, men jeg ved ikke, hvor hun bor." (Also a noun: en kender = an expert, connoisseur.)

ligge.summary: Lie, be (located) — for flat things and places. Pair: lægge = put (flat).

uses.da_en: The keys are on the table.

ligge.note: Forms: ligge · ligger · lå · har ligget. Moving something there is lægge: "Jeg lægger nøglerne på bordet." Upright things stå; attached or seated things sidde.

lægge.summary: Put, lay (flat) — the action. Pair: ligge = be lying / be located.

uses.da_en: I'm putting the keys on the table.

uses.da: Jeg lægger mig lidt på sofaen.
uses.da_en: I'm going to lie down on the sofa for a bit.

uses.da: Lagde du mærke til hans sko?

lægge.note: Forms: lægge · lægger · lagde · har lagt. Test: is something being moved? lægge. Is it just there? ligge. Even Danes mix them up.

sidde.summary: Sit, be sitting — also "be" for things that are stuck or attached. Pair: sætte = put / sit down.

uses.da: Hun sidder i sofaen og læser.
uses.da_en: She's sitting on the sofa reading.

sidde.note: Forms: sidde · sidder · sad · har siddet. "Sit down!" is normally "Sæt dig (ned)!" ("Sid ned!" is heard in casual speech). Danes sit i (in) a sofa.

sætte.summary: Put, place, set — and sætte sig = sit down. Pair: sidde = be sitting.

uses.da_en: I put the cup in the dishwasher.

uses.da: Jeg sætter stor pris på din hjælp.

sætte.note: Forms: sætte · sætter · satte · har sat. Put upright: stille; put flat: lægge; put into something (casual): putte.

stå.summary: Stand, be standing — also "be" for upright things, and "say" for written text.

uses.da: Der står, at butikken lukker klokken 18.
uses.da_en: It says the shop closes at 6.

uses.da: Jeg står af ved næste stop.
uses.da_en: I'm getting off at the next stop.

stå.note: Forms: stå · står · stod · har stået. Putting something upright is stille: "Stil flasken på bordet." "Hvad står der?" = What does it say?

stille.summary: Two words: the verb "put (upright)" and the adjective "quiet, still".

uses.da_en: Put the bottle on the table.

stille.note: Verb: stille · stiller · stillede · har stillet. Pair: stå = be standing. "Stille og roligt" = calmly, take it easy.

lære.summary: Learn — and, with a person, teach. One verb does both:

uses.da_en: I'm learning Danish at a language school.

uses.da: Min far lærte mig at cykle.
uses.da_en: My dad taught me to ride a bike.

uses.da: Vi lærte hinanden at kende på arbejdet.
uses.da_en: We got to know each other at work.

lære.note: Forms: lære · lærer · lærte · har lært. en lærer = a teacher (lærer is also "learns / teaches"). en underviser = a teacher, lecturer.

lærer.summary: Learn — and, with a person, teach. One verb does both:

uses.da_en: I'm learning Danish at a language school.

uses.da: Min far lærte mig at cykle.
uses.da_en: My dad taught me to ride a bike.

uses.da: Vi lærte hinanden at kende på arbejdet.
uses.da_en: We got to know each other at work.

lærer.note: Forms: lære · lærer · lærte · har lært. en lærer = a teacher (lærer is also "learns / teaches"). en underviser = a teacher, lecturer.

undervise.summary: Teach (a class or subject) — as a job. Takes i before the subject.

uses.da_en: He teaches adults in the evenings.

undervise.note: Forms: undervise · underviser · underviste · har undervist. en underviser = a teacher, lecturer; undervisning = teaching, lessons.

låne.summary: Both borrow AND lend — the little words decide which:

uses.da: Jeg lånte en cykel af min nabo.
uses.da_en: I borrowed a bike from my neighbour.

uses.da: Jeg har lånt min bil ud til min søster.
uses.da_en: I've lent my car to my sister.

uses.en: thanks for letting me borrow it
uses.da: Her er din bog. Tak for lån!
uses.da_en: Here's your book. Thanks for lending it to me!

låne.note: Forms: låne · låner · lånte · har lånt. From a person: låne af, not fra. et lån = a loan.

høre.summary: Hear and listen — and also "ask, check":

uses.da_en: I listen to music on the train.

uses.da: Jeg ville bare høre, om du vil med.
uses.da_en: I just wanted to ask if you'd like to come.

uses.da: Hør her, jeg har en idé.

høre.note: Forms: høre · hører · hørte · har hørt. "Det kan jeg høre" = I can tell (from what you say). "høre efter" = pay attention.

mangle.summary: Lack, be missing — Danes use it where English says "need":

uses.da: Tak for hjælpen! – Det manglede bare.
uses.da_en: Thanks for the help! – Don't mention it.

mangle.note: Forms: mangle · mangler · manglede · har manglet. Other ways to say need: have brug for, trænge til ("Bilen trænger til at blive vasket" = The car needs washing).

tænke.summary: Think — as an activity (thinking about, considering). An opinion is synes; a guess is tror:

uses.da: Kunne du tænke dig en kop te?
uses.da_en: Would you like a cup of tea?

uses.da: Jeg har tænkt mig at flytte.
Jeg tænkte på, om du ville med?
uses.da_en: I was wondering if you'd like to come?

tænke.note: Forms: tænke · tænker · tænkte · har tænkt. "Jeg tænker, at …" for an opinion is common now, but some Danes dislike it; synes is always safe. (en tænker = a thinker.)

tænker.summary: Think — as an activity (thinking about, considering). An opinion is synes; a guess is tror:

uses.da: Kunne du tænke dig en kop te?
uses.da_en: Would you like a cup of tea?

uses.da: Jeg har tænkt mig at flytte.
Jeg tænkte på, om du ville med?
uses.da_en: I was wondering if you'd like to come?

tænker.note: Forms: tænke · tænker · tænkte · har tænkt. "Jeg tænker, at …" for an opinion is common now, but some Danes dislike it; synes is always safe. (en tænker = a thinker.)

gå.summary: Walk, go on foot — plus many fixed phrases. Travelling by vehicle is tage, køre or rejse:

uses.en: that won't work / that's not OK
uses.da: Det går ikke, jeg har ikke tid.
uses.da_en: That won't work, I don't have time.

uses.da: Jeg går til dansk om tirsdagen.
uses.da_en: I go to Danish classes on Tuesdays.

gå.note: Travel: "Jeg tager til London", not "går". Perfect: "Han er gået" (he's left) vs "Han har gået meget" (he's walked a lot). Forms: gå · går · gik · er/har gået. Don't mix up går (goes) and gør (does). Also gå på arbejde, gå i seng.

går.summary: Walk, go on foot — plus many fixed phrases. Travelling by vehicle is tage, køre or rejse:

uses.en: that won't work / that's not OK
uses.da: Det går ikke, jeg har ikke tid.
uses.da_en: That won't work, I don't have time.

uses.da: Jeg går til dansk om tirsdagen.
uses.da_en: I go to Danish classes on Tuesdays.

går.note: Travel: "Jeg tager til London", not "går". Perfect: "Han er gået" (he's left) vs "Han har gået meget" (he's walked a lot). Forms: gå · går · gik · er/har gået. Don't mix up går (goes) and gør (does). Also gå på arbejde, gå i seng.

tage.summary: Take — but also "have" when ordering and "go" when travelling:

uses.da_en: We're taking the train to Aarhus.
Do you want to come along?

tage.note: Forms: tage · tager · tog · har taget (often said "ta'"). tage til = go to (a place); tage på ferie = go on holiday.

få.summary: Get — with several uses English says differently. Also the adjective "few":

uses.da_en: What are we having for dinner?

uses.da: Hun fik lov til at gå tidligt.
uses.da_en: She was allowed to leave early.
I finally got round to tidying up.

få.note: Forms: få · får · fik · har fået. "Get + adjective" is blive (blive træt), not få. "Vi får se" = We'll see. See får for more.

gide.summary: Can be bothered (to) — see gider for the everyday uses.

uses.da: Jeg gad ikke gå ud i går.
uses.da_en: I couldn't be bothered to go out yesterday.

uses.en: I'd love to know, I wonder
uses.da: Jeg gad godt vide, hvad der skete.
uses.da_en: I'd love to know what happened.

gide.note: Forms: gide · gider · gad · har gidet. Casual; no "at" before the next verb.

turde.summary: Dare — present tør, past turde, perfect har turdet:

uses.da_en: Are you brave enough to jump?

uses.da: Jeg turde ikke sige det til ham.

turde.note: No "at" after it. Don't confuse with tørre (to dry: tørrede = dried) or the adjective tør (dry).

burde.summary: Should, ought to — the past and softer form of bør:

uses.da_en: You ought to take a break.

burde.note: Forms: burde · bør · burde · har burdet. No "at" after it.

pleje.summary: Two meanings: plejer at = usually (a habit), and pleje = care for, nurse:

uses.da: Hvad plejer du at lave om søndagen?
uses.da_en: What do you usually do on Sundays?
She's looking after her sick mother.

pleje.note: Habit needs "at" + a verb; without it, pleje means caring. Past plejede (at) = used to. See plejer.

virke.note: A job is arbejde: "Jeg arbejder hos Novo." Forms: virke · virker · virkede · har virket.

passe.summary: Fit, suit, look after — and "be true":

uses.da_en: She looks after children in the afternoons.

passe.note: Forms: passe · passer · passede · har passet. "Pas godt på dig selv!" = Take good care of yourself!

passer.summary: Fit, suit, look after — and "be true":

uses.da_en: She looks after children in the afternoons.

passer.note: Forms: passe · passer · passede · har passet. "Pas godt på dig selv!" = Take good care of yourself!

tabe.summary: Lose — mainly drop, lose a game, lose weight. Losing something for good is often miste:

uses.da: Jeg tabte min telefon på gulvet.
uses.da_en: I dropped my phone on the floor.

tabe.note: Forms: tabe · taber · tabte · har tabt. en taber = a loser. miste = no longer have: "miste sit job".

taber.summary: Lose — mainly drop, lose a game, lose weight. Losing something for good is often miste:

uses.da: Jeg tabte min telefon på gulvet.
uses.da_en: I dropped my phone on the floor.

taber.note: Forms: tabe · taber · tabte · har tabt. en taber = a loser. miste = no longer have: "miste sit job".

miste.summary: Lose — no longer have (a person, a job, a chance). Dropping things or losing a match is tabe:

uses.da: Hun mistede sin far sidste år.
uses.da_en: She lost her father last year.

miste.note: Forms: miste · mister · mistede · har mistet.

bo.summary: Live — where you live (reside). Being alive, or how you live, is leve:

uses.da: Hun bor sammen med sin kæreste.

bo.note: "Jeg lever i Odense" sounds like "I exist / survive in Odense". Forms: bo · bor · boede · har boet. (en bor = a drill.)

bor.summary: Live — where you live (reside). Being alive, or how you live, is leve:

uses.da: Hun bor sammen med sin kæreste.

bor.note: "Jeg lever i Odense" sounds like "I exist / survive in Odense". Forms: bo · bor · boede · har boet. (en bor = a drill.)

leve.summary: Live — be alive, lead a life. Where you live (your address) is bo:

uses.en: live on, make a living from
uses.da_en: He makes a living from writing.

leve.note: Forms: leve · lever · levede · har levet. (en lever = a liver.)

lever.summary: Live — be alive, lead a life. Where you live (your address) is bo:

uses.en: live on, make a living from
uses.da_en: He makes a living from writing.

lever.note: Forms: leve · lever · levede · har levet. (en lever = a liver.)

hilse.summary: Greet — and the everyday way to pass on greetings:

uses.da_en: Say hi to your mum for me!

uses.da: Kom og hils på min bror.

hilse.note: Forms: hilse · hilser · hilste · har hilst; command: hils. en hilsen = a greeting; "Med venlig hilsen" = Kind regards.

nemlig.summary: Gives the reason after the fact — "you see" — and a quick "exactly!":

uses.da: Jeg tager bussen. Min cykel er nemlig punkteret.
uses.da_en: I'm taking the bus — my bike's got a flat, you see.

uses.da: Så vi skal til venstre? – Nemlig!
Han har to hobbyer, nemlig golf og vin.
uses.da_en: He has two hobbies, namely golf and wine.

nemlig.note: It sits after the verb like ikke ("Jeg er nemlig syg") — never first like English "because".

alligevel.summary: After all, anyway, still — the plan or expectation changed. Not the topic-changing "Anyway, …":

uses.da: Det regnede, men vi gik en tur alligevel.
uses.da_en: It was raining, but we went for a walk anyway.

uses.da: Jeg kan godt hente den, jeg skal alligevel i byen.
uses.da_en: I can pick it up — I'm going into town anyway.

uses.da: Han er streng, men alligevel ret sød.
uses.da_en: He's strict, but still quite nice.

alligevel.note: To change the subject ("Anyway, …") say "Nå, men …" or "Men i hvert fald …".

egentlig.summary: Actually, really — softens a statement, or makes a question friendly-curious:

uses.da_en: Strictly speaking I should be working, but …

egentlig.note: A question with egentlig is curious, not challenging. faktisk insists more that something IS so; in casual speech the two overlap. Both g's are silent.

faktisk.summary: Actually, in fact — it really IS so, often against expectation:

uses.da: Jeg har faktisk aldrig været i Aarhus.
uses.da_en: I've actually never been to Aarhus.

faktisk.note: Not the English word — aktuel / aktuelt = current, topical — not "actually". egentlig = deep down, in principle; faktisk = in fact.

selv.summary: Self — but also "even", "by yourself" and the polite "selv tak":

uses.da_en: Can you manage on your own?

uses.da: Selv om det regner, går vi en tur.
uses.da_en: Even though it's raining, we're going for a walk.

uses.da: Tak for i aften! – Selv tak!
uses.da_en: Thanks for this evening! – Thank you!

selv.note: The ordinary reflexive "himself" is sig: "Han vasker sig". Add selv only for emphasis: "Han vasker sig selv" (himself, not someone else). selv ikke = not even.

også.summary: Also, too — but in a negative sentence Danes switch to heller ikke:

uses.da: Jeg kan også godt lide jazz.

uses.en: so do I / so am I
uses.da: Jeg er træt. – Det er jeg også.
Jeg kan heller ikke lide jazz.
Det var en god film, ikke også?
uses.da_en: That was a good film, wasn't it?

også.note: Never "også ikke". Often pronounced just "os". Altså is not English "also".

heller.summary: Used in heller ikke = not … either, neither. (hellere = rather is a separate word.)

uses.en: neither do I / neither have I
uses.da: Jeg har ikke set den. – Det har jeg heller ikke.
uses.da_en: I haven't seen it. – Neither have I.

uses.da: Jeg gider ikke. – Heller ikke mig.
uses.da_en: I can't be bothered. – Me neither.

heller.note: The positive version is også: "Det har jeg også" (So have I). Never "også ikke".

hellere.summary: Rather — the comparative of gerne (gerne · hellere · helst):

uses.da: Jeg tager hellere toget end bilen.
uses.da_en: I'd rather take the train than the car.

uses.da: Jeg vil helst ikke tale om det.
uses.da_en: I'd rather not talk about it.

hellere.note: "Det må jeg nok hellere" = I'd better (do that).

bare.summary: Just, only — and a warm "go ahead":

uses.da: Bare rolig, det skal nok gå.
Du må gerne låne den, bare du passer på den.
uses.da_en: You can borrow it, as long as you look after it.

bare.note: "Tag bare!" = Help yourself! — friendly encouragement, not dismissive.

sådan.summary: Such, like that, that way — and "There we go!":

uses.da: Jeg vil også gerne have sådan en.
uses.da_en: I'd like one of those too.

uses.en: something like that, that kind of thing
uses.da_en: Do you like that kind of thing?

sådan.note: "Det er bare sådan" = That's just how it is. sådan her = like this; sådan der = like that.

nå.summary: Two words: the reaction "oh / well" (tone decides) and the verb "reach, make it":

uses.da: Hun er syg i dag. – Nåh, okay.
uses.da_en: She's ill today. – Oh, I see.

nå.note: A flat "nå" can mean "Oh. Whatever." Verb forms: nå · når · nåede · har nået — so når can be "reaches" as well as "when".

nu.summary: Now — but unstressed it softens ("actually"), and in questions it means "again":

uses.da: Det er nu ikke så dumt.
uses.da_en: That's actually not a bad idea.

uses.da: Nu hvor du er her, kan du hjælpe mig.
uses.da_en: Now that you're here, you can help me.

nu.note: lige nu = right now; nu og da = now and then.

skam.summary: Shame — but as an unstressed little word it means "indeed, I assure you":

uses.da: Det er en skam, at du ikke kan komme.
uses.da_en: It's a pity you can't come.

skam.note: The reassuring skam is positive: "Det smager skam godt" = It actually tastes good, you know.

sikkert.summary: Usually "probably" — a hedge. For "definitely" Danes say helt sikkert:

uses.da_en: He'll probably come a bit later.

uses.da: Er det sikkert at bade her?
uses.da_en: Is it safe to swim here?

sikkert.note: "Jeg kommer sikkert" is a maybe, not a promise. sikker (adj.) = sure, certain ("Er du sikker?") or safe.

først.summary: First — and also "not until", which English speakers often miss:

uses.da: Først spiser vi, og så går vi en tur.
uses.da_en: First we'll eat, and then we'll go for a walk.

uses.da: Jeg har først ferie om en måned.
uses.da_en: I'm not on holiday for another month.

uses.da: Først og fremmest vil jeg sige tak.
uses.da_en: First of all, I'd like to say thank you.

først.note: "Han kommer først i morgen" = He won't come till tomorrow. den første = the first one; for det første = firstly.

endnu.summary: Yet — and "even" before a comparative. For "still" use stadig:

uses.da: I morgen bliver det endnu varmere.
Skal vi tage endnu en øl?

uses.da_en: Do you still live in Odense?

ellers.summary: Otherwise, or else — and two polite shop phrases:

uses.da: Skynd dig, ellers kommer vi for sent.
uses.da_en: Hurry up, or we'll be late.

uses.da: Ellers andet? – Nej tak, det var det hele.
uses.da_en: Anything else? – No thanks, that's everything.

uses.da: Vil du have mere kaffe? – Ellers tak.

ellers.note: "Ellers tak" looks like "otherwise thanks" but it is a polite NO.

rigtig.summary: Right, correct — and very often REALLY (before an adjective):
rigtig.note: Forms: rigtig · rigtigt · rigtige. "You're right" is "Du har ret" (not rigtig). rigtig mange = a great many.

ret.summary: Several words: quite/rather, have ret (be right), a dish, and a right:

uses.da: Du har ret til at sige nej.
uses.da_en: You have the right to say no.

ret.note: en ret (dish), plural retter; en ret (right), plural rettigheder. retten = the court.

så.summary: One of the busiest little words: then, so, so (very) — and the past of se (saw):

uses.da: Først spiser vi, og så går vi.
uses.da_en: First we eat, then we go.

uses.da: Hvis det regner, så tager jeg bussen.
uses.da_en: If it rains, I'll take the bus.

uses.da: Jeg er syg, så jeg kan ikke komme.
uses.da_en: I'm ill, so I can't come.

uses.da: Jeg er så træt i dag.
Jeg så en god film i går.
uses.da_en: I saw a good film yesterday.

så.note: så = "then" is followed by the verb: "og så går vi". så = "so (result)" is followed by the subject: "så jeg kan ikke komme". så … at = so … that.

værsgo.summary: From "vær så god" (be so good). Said when you give, offer or invite:

uses.en: here you are, here you go
uses.da_en: Here you go, here's your coffee.

værsgo.note: Also spelled værsågod. When serving food you say værsgo; velbekomme is mainly the reply to "tak for mad".

velbekomme.summary: The reply to "tak for mad" — no English word; roughly "you're welcome, glad you enjoyed it".

uses.en: you're welcome, glad you liked it
uses.da_en: Thanks for the meal! – You're welcome.

uses.en: be my guest, good luck with that
uses.da_en: He wants to pay himself? Be my guest!

velbekomme.note: Not mainly "bon appétit": its core use is AFTER the meal. When putting food on the table Danes usually say værsgo.

uses.da: Han udbragte en skål for brudeparret.
uses.da_en: He proposed a toast to the bride and groom.

skål.note: At the table, look people in the eye when you say skål, drink, and look again before putting the glass down; the host usually makes the first toast.

fyraften.summary: The moment the working day ends — at any time of day. No single English word:

uses.da_en: What time do you finish work?

uses.en: call it a day, knock off

uses.da_en: Shall we grab an after-work beer?

fyraften.note: Not "evening": a shift worker can have fyraften at 2 pm. Leaving work on time is normal and expected.

undskyld.summary: Sorry AND excuse me — the quick everyday apology and attention-getter:

uses.da: Undskyld, at jeg kommer for sent.

undskyld.note: "Jeg er ked af det" means "I'm sad / upset" — use it for real regret or sympathy, not for bumping into someone. Verb: undskylde; "Du må undskylde" = please forgive me.

ked.summary: Used in ked af: sad, upset — or sorry about something. Not a quick "sorry":

uses.da: Hun er ked af det, fordi hendes kat er død.
uses.da_en: She's upset because her cat died.

uses.da: Jeg er ked af, at jeg ikke kunne komme.
Jeg er virkelig ked af at høre det.
uses.da_en: I'm really sorry to hear that.

ked.note: A quick apology is undskyld. Don't mix it up with træt af (fed up with).

ærgerlig.summary: Annoying in a disappointing way — "what a shame", not "angry":

uses.da: Koncerten er aflyst. – Det var ærgerligt.
uses.da_en: The concert's cancelled. – That's a shame.

uses.da: Han var ærgerlig over, at han tabte.
uses.da_en: He was annoyed that he lost.

uses.da: Jeg ærgrer mig over, at jeg ikke købte billetter.
uses.da_en: I'm kicking myself for not buying tickets.

ærgerlig.note: "Øv!" = Bummer! (small disappointments). Angry is vred; cross is sur.

sur.summary: Sour — and, about people, cross or grumpy:

uses.da: Han blev sur, fordi han tabte.
uses.da_en: He got grumpy because he lost.

sur.note: sur på nogen = cross with someone. vred = angry (stronger). Forms: sur · surt · sure.

kæreste.summary: Boyfriend, girlfriend or partner — one gender-neutral word, at any age:

uses.da: Min kæreste og jeg har boet sammen i ti år.
uses.da_en: My partner and I have lived together for ten years.

uses.da: De har været kærester siden gymnasiet.
uses.da_en: They've been together since high school.

kæreste.note: A friend is en ven / en veninde (female), not kæreste. Also the superlative of kær: "min kæreste ven" = my dearest friend.

sympatisk.summary: Not the English word — likeable, pleasant — not "sympathetic" (that's forstående or medfølende).
sympatisk.note: "She was very sympathetic" (understanding) = "Hun var meget forstående."

tryg.summary: Feeling safe, secure, at ease — the feeling, not physical safety:

uses.da_en: The children feel secure at nursery.
Savings give you peace of mind.

tryg.note: Physical safety is sikker / sikkerhed: "Er det sikkert at bade her?" Forms: tryg · trygt · trygge.

pålæg.summary: Anything you put on bread — no single English word:

uses.en: sandwich toppings: cold cuts, cheese, spreads
uses.da: Hvad vil du have som pålæg?
uses.da_en: What do you want on your bread?

uses.da: Vi har ost, leverpostej og andet pålæg.
uses.da_en: We have cheese, liver pâté and other toppings.

pålæg.note: et pålæg. Includes meat, cheese, egg, spreads — even pålægschokolade (thin chocolate slices for bread).

overskud.summary: Surplus — and, very often, personal energy or headspace to spare:

uses.da: Jeg har ikke overskud til at tage med i aften.
uses.da_en: I don't have the energy to come along tonight.

uses.en: energy to spare, on top of things
uses.da: Hun har meget overskud, selvom hun har tre små børn.
uses.da_en: She has lots of energy to spare, even with three small kids.
The company made a profit last year.

overskud.note: Danes say "Jeg har ikke overskud" where English says "I'm not up to it" or "I don't have the bandwidth". Opposite: underskud = deficit.

overskue.summary: Get an overview of — and, in everyday speech, "cope with, face":

uses.en: can't face it, it's too much right now
uses.da: Jeg kan ikke overskue at flytte lige nu.
uses.da_en: I can't face moving right now.

uses.da: Kun tre uger tilbage – det er til at overskue.
uses.da_en: Only three weeks left – that's manageable.

uses.da: Det er svært at overskue konsekvenserne.
uses.da_en: It's hard to foresee the consequences.

overskue.note: Not "oversee" (supervise = lede, føre tilsyn med). overskuelig = manageable, clear; uoverskuelig = overwhelming.

overblik.summary: Overview, the big picture — being on top of things:

uses.da: Jeg skal lige have overblik over budgettet.
uses.da_en: I just need to get a clear picture of the budget.

gang.summary: Danish "time" as in occasion — and several other jobs:

uses.da: Det er første gang, jeg er i Aarhus.
uses.da_en: It's the first time I've been to Aarhus.

uses.da: Jeg træner tre gange om ugen.
uses.da_en: I work out three times a week.

uses.da: Nogle gange cykler jeg på arbejde.

uses.en: be busy with, be in the middle of
uses.da: Jeg er i gang med at lave mad.
uses.da_en: I'm in the middle of cooking.
The coats are out in the hall.

gang.note: en gang = one time, once; engang (one word) = once upon a time, some day. en gang til = once more. An hour is en time; clock time is klokken.

time.summary: Not the English word — en time = an HOUR (or a lesson, an appointment) — not "time":

uses.da: Jeg har en time hos tandlægen i morgen.
uses.da_en: I've got a dentist's appointment tomorrow.

time.note: An occasion ("the first time") is gang: første gang. Forms: en time · timen · timer.

lækker.summary: Delicious — but also gorgeous for things, and hot for people:
lækker.note: Forms: lækker · lækkert · lækre. About people it's about looks — careful at work. Not the English word — not "leaky".

sød.summary: Sweet — and very often KIND or CUTE. Also the key to saying "please":

uses.da: Hun er så sød ved børnene.
uses.da_en: She's so kind to the kids.

uses.da: Hvor er det sødt af dig!
Vil du være sød at lukke vinduet?
uses.da_en: Would you please close the window?
The cake is far too sweet.

sød.note: "Du er sød" usually means "you're kind", not a romantic hint. "Sov sødt" = sleep well. Forms: sød · sødt · søde.

dejlig.summary: Lovely — the all-purpose word for something pleasant:

uses.da: Det er dejligt vejr i dag.
Tak for mad, det var dejligt.
uses.da_en: Thanks for the meal, it was delicious.
The water is nice and warm.

dejlig.note: Forms: dejlig · dejligt · dejlige. Of a person, dejlig = lovely (broad, warm); lækker = hot. See also sød, flink, hyggelig.

flink.summary: Nice, kind, helpful — one of several Danish words for English "nice":
flink.note: Pick by meaning: helpful/kind = flink; kind/cute = sød; pleasant company = hyggelig; good-looking/neat = pæn; lovely = dejlig. Forms: flink · flinkt · flinke.

pæn.summary: Nice-LOOKING, neat, decent — about looks and manners, not kindness:

uses.da: Du ser pæn ud i dag.
Hun tjener en pæn sum penge.

pæn.note: For kind people use flink or sød. Forms: pæn · pænt · pæne.

sjov.summary: Fun AND funny AND odd — context decides:

uses.da: Det var sjovt at være med!
Det er sjovt, at du siger det.
uses.da_en: It's funny you should say that.

sjov.note: Forms: sjov · sjovt · sjove. sjovt nok = funnily enough. For a clear "funny ha-ha" Danes also say morsom or skæg.

uses.da: Mærkeligt nok var der ingen hjemme.

mærkelig.note: Close: underlig (odd). sær is more judgemental about people (eccentric, a bit off). Forms: mærkelig · mærkeligt · mærkelige.

fuld.summary: Full — and very often DRUNK. After a meal you're mæt, not fuld:

uses.da_en: He was drunk at the party.

uses.da: Kassen er fuld af gammelt legetøj.
uses.da_en: The box is full of old toys.

fuld.note: Saying "Jeg er fuld" after dinner means "I'm drunk"! Forms: fuld · fuldt · fulde. fuldtid = full-time.

færdig.summary: Finished, ready — and, about people, exhausted:

uses.da_en: Are you done with the paper?

uses.da: Maden er færdig om ti minutter.
uses.da_en: The food will be ready in ten minutes.

uses.da: Jeg er helt færdig efter i dag.
uses.da_en: I'm completely worn out after today.

færdig.note: færdig med = finished with, done with. Forms: færdig · færdigt · færdige. klar = ready (to go).

frisk.summary: Fresh — and, about people, well, lively, up for it:

uses.da: Er du frisk på en øl?

frisk.note: Forms: frisk · friskt · friske. "Frisk på" is casual.

på.summary: "On" — but very often "at" or "in", chosen by convention. Learn it in phrases:

uses.da: Hun er på arbejde til klokken fem.

på.note: Also på hospitalet, på biblioteket, på ferie (on holiday), på vej (on the way), tænke på (think about), tro på (believe in), passe på (look after). Last Friday = i fredags.

i.summary: "In" — but also "for" with time spans, and part of most time words. (Capital I = you, plural.)

uses.da: Jeg har boet her i tre år.
uses.da_en: I've lived here for three years.

uses.da: i dag, i går, i morgen, i aften
Jeg var i biografen i fredags.
uses.da_en: I went to the cinema last Friday.

uses.da: Hvad skal I lave i weekenden?
uses.da_en: What are you all doing this weekend?

i.note: i nat = last night OR tonight; i morges = this morning (past). "In ten minutes" (future) is om ti minutter, not i. i sofaen = on the sofa.

til.summary: "To" for movement — and "for" or "at" in many fixed phrases:

uses.da: Vi var til fest i lørdags.
uses.da_en: We were at a party on Saturday.

uses.da: Hvad skal vi have til aftensmad?
uses.da_en: What are we having for dinner?

uses.da: Hvad skal I lave til jul?
uses.da_en: What are you doing for Christmas?

uses.da: Jeg glæder mig til at se dig.
uses.da_en: I'm looking forward to seeing you.

til.note: Going = til; being there = hos / i / på: "Jeg er hos lægen." Also til tiden (on time), til venstre (to the left), til salg (for sale), gå til dansk (attend Danish classes).

uses.da: Jeg flyttede hertil for tre år siden.
uses.da_en: I moved here three years ago.

uses.da: Jeg går i seng, for jeg er træt.
uses.da_en: I'm going to bed, because I'm tired.

for.note: "For two hours" is i to timer, not for to timer. for sent = late; for meget = too much; glad for = happy with, fond of. Wait for = vente på; ask for = bede om.

af.summary: "Of" and "by" — plus "from" and "off" in fixed phrases:

uses.da: Bogen er skrevet af en dansker.
uses.da_en: The book was written by a Dane.

uses.da: Jeg fik den af min bror.
uses.da_en: I got it from my brother.
I'm fed up with the rain.

uses.da: Jeg står af ved næste stop.
uses.da_en: I'm getting off at the next stop.
The table is made of wood.

af.note: ked af det = sad; af og til = now and then; låne af = borrow from.

med.summary: With — and "by" (transport), and "along" (joining in) with no verb:

uses.da: Jeg bor sammen med min kæreste.

uses.da_en: Are you done with the washing-up?

med.note: være med = take part; tage med = come along / bring; vild med = crazy about.

om.summary: About, in (future time), on (habits) — and "whether / if":

uses.da_en: The train leaves in ten minutes.

uses.da: Jeg ved ikke, om han kommer.
uses.da_en: I don't know if he's coming.
Could I have the bill, please?

om.note: "If" as a condition is hvis: "Hvis det regner …". Use om when you could say "whether".

hvis.summary: If — a condition. For "if" meaning "whether" use om. Also "whose":

uses.da: Hvis det regner, bliver vi hjemme.
uses.da_en: If it rains, we'll stay home.

uses.da: Spørg hende, om hun vil med.
uses.da_en: Ask her if she wants to come.

uses.da: Hvis jeg var dig, ville jeg tage jobbet.
uses.da_en: If I were you, I'd take the job.

hvis.note: Test: if you could say "whether", it's om. After hvis and om, ikke comes before the verb: "hvis han ikke kommer".

når.summary: When — for something repeated or still to come. One past event takes da; a question takes hvornår:

uses.da: Når jeg kommer hjem, ringer jeg.
uses.da_en: When I get home, I'll call.

uses.da: Når det regnede, blev vi inde.
uses.da_en: Whenever it rained, we stayed in.

uses.da: Da jeg mødte hende, var hun 20.
uses.da_en: When I met her, she was 20.

når.note: Test: "that one time in the past" = da; "every time" or not happened yet = når. når is also the present of nå (reach): "Vi når det" = We'll make it.

hvornår.summary: When? — only in questions, including indirect ones:

uses.da: Jeg ved ikke, hvornår filmen starter.
uses.da_en: I don't know when the film starts.

hvornår.note: In a statement, "when" is når (future or repeated) or da (one past event).

siden.summary: Since — and part of "ago" (for … siden). Also "the side / the page":

uses.da: Vi mødtes for fem år siden.

siden.note: "For three years" is i tre år. siden is also the side / the page (side + -n).

hjem.summary: Home — going there (movement). Being at home is hjemme:

uses.da: Vil du med hjem til mig?
uses.da_en: Do you want to come back to my place?

hjem.note: Short form = movement, long form = being there: hjem/hjemme, ud/ude, ind/inde, op/oppe, ned/nede, hen/henne.

hjemme.summary: At home — being there (no movement). Going home is hjem:
hjemme.note: "Jeg går hjemme" = I'm at home (not working) — going home is "Jeg går hjem". hjemmeside = website. Short form = movement, long form = being there: hjem/hjemme, ud/ude, ind/inde, op/oppe, ned/nede, hen/henne.

ud.summary: Out — movement outwards. Being outside is ude:

uses.da: Jeg går lige ud med skraldet.
uses.da_en: I'm just taking the rubbish out.

uses.da: Skal vi tage ud og spise?
uses.da_en: Shall we go out to eat?

ud.note: Short form = movement, long form = being there: hjem/hjemme, ud/ude, ind/inde, op/oppe, ned/nede, hen/henne.

ude.summary: Out, outside — being there. Going out is ud:
ude.note: Short form = movement, long form = being there: hjem/hjemme, ud/ude, ind/inde, op/oppe, ned/nede, hen/henne.

ind.summary: In — movement inwards. Being inside is inde:

uses.da_en: She went into the living room.

uses.da: Vi flytter ind i næste uge.

ind.note: Short form = movement, long form = being there: hjem/hjemme, ud/ude, ind/inde, op/oppe, ned/nede, hen/henne.

inde.summary: In, inside — being there. Going in is ind:
inde.note: Short form = movement, long form = being there: hjem/hjemme, ud/ude, ind/inde, op/oppe, ned/nede, hen/henne.

op.summary: Up — movement upwards. Being up there is oppe:
op.note: Short form = movement, long form = being there: hjem/hjemme, ud/ude, ind/inde, op/oppe, ned/nede, hen/henne.

oppe.summary: Up, upstairs — being there. Going up is op:
oppe.note: Short form = movement, long form = being there: hjem/hjemme, ud/ude, ind/inde, op/oppe, ned/nede, hen/henne.

ned.summary: Down — movement downwards. Being down there is nede:

uses.da_en: He went down to the basement.

ned.note: Short form = movement, long form = being there: hjem/hjemme, ud/ude, ind/inde, op/oppe, ned/nede, hen/henne.

nede.summary: Down, downstairs — being there. Going down is ned:

uses.da_en: The bike's down in the basement.

uses.da: Han er lidt nede i dag.

nede.note: Short form = movement, long form = being there: hjem/hjemme, ud/ude, ind/inde, op/oppe, ned/nede, hen/henne.

hen.summary: Over (to) — movement toward a place; often left untranslated. Being there is henne:

uses.da: Jeg går lige hen til bageren.
uses.da_en: I'm just popping over to the baker's.

hen.note: derhen = (to) there. Short form = movement, long form = being there: hjem/hjemme, ud/ude, ind/inde, op/oppe, ned/nede, hen/henne.
